newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany hooked on debt, stability at risk - study.
newsitem.headline: Germany hooked on debt, stability at risk - study.

text.p: Germany is hooked on living beyond its means, jeopardising its fitness for European monetary union and risking eventual destabilisation in its economy and society, a prominent think-tank said in a study on Tuesday.
In "Living on Credit", the Institute of Economy and Society (IWG) says Germany will struggle to meet both the Maastricht treaty criteria on public debt and new borrowing next year.

And without tough action to bring state welfare and pension schemes under control, Germany cannot hold to the Maastricht limits in the long run, it said. Spending cuts just introduced by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government were not enough.
"An extreme debt avalanche has started moving which we can't yet see," IWG head Professor Meinhard Miegel warned at a news conference called to present the study.
Miegel said that monetary union would probably go ahead, but to do so the Maastricht criteria would have to be applied loosely when it came to debt limits.
Germany's debt has exploded since World War II, from 20 billion marks in 1949 to 900 billion marks in 1989, and doubling again since unification to 1.9 trillion marks.

Debt expressed as a percentage of gross domestic product now exceeds 60 percent -- the Maastricht target -- and if no action is taken could hit 70 percent by 2005. Maastricht sets a budget deficit goal of at or near three percent of GDP.

The willingness of current leaders to run up state debts will end in a day of reckoning with the next generation, which will have to pick up the tab for their profligacy, study author Adrian Ottnad said.

"Growing state debt is...the result of and reinforces a breakdown of social solidarity," Ottnad said. He added that the only way to break the vicious circle is to set a constitutional limit on state borrowing of one percent of GDP per year.
Assuming favourable growth of a nominal 4.5 percent per year up to the year 2005, it could be possible to hold the debt ratio at around current levels, the study said.

But, taking into account the "hidden debt" in the social security and pensions systems of at least an additional 150 percent of GDP, a drastic rise in real borrowing must be expected to cover top-ups in welfare funding shortfalls.
Ottnad warned of the risks of doing nothing.

"The negative consequences have long-since become apparent: A loss of the state's ability to act, losses in growth and jobs, rising taxes and social burdens, destabilisation of the monetary, political and social order and growing tensions between young and old."
Miegel blamed the malaise on the "addiction to wealth" of a "me-first" generation expecting to be pampered by the state.
Citizens want more services than they are prepared to finance, and politicians and parties pander to those demands in return for votes.

That has led to a "collective overburdening of the state", which has coincided with a surge in tax evasion. Legal and illegal tax avoidance totals around 150 billion marks -- equal to around half total income tax revenues, Ottnad said.
But it is not too late to wean people off an all-providing state for which they are not prepared to pay.

Assuming nominal annual GDP growth of five percent and an average budget deficit of two percent, it could be possible to cut back public debt to 50 percent of GDP by 2005 while passing moderate cuts in taxes and social security costs, Ottnad said.
